fun_facts: A tarpon rolling at the surface usually isn't playing: it's gulping a mouthful of air into a modified swim bladder that works like a crude lung, letting it pull oxygen straight from the atmosphere in water too stagnant for gilled fish to survive in.

A tarpon can live 50 years, possibly past 70, but it doesn't reach sexual maturity until roughly its tenth year -- most of the giants caught and released off South Carolina are older than the anglers catching them.
For a fish tough enough to survive nearly oxygen-free water, tarpon are surprisingly fragile to cold: a hard snap that drops coastal water below about 50°F can cold-stun and kill them outright.

measures.label: Total length
measures.help: Tip of the lower jaw to the tip of the tail, fish laid flat and straight.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Tarpon cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: tarpon have been a protected game fish in South Carolina since 1991: no harvest or possession is allowed under state law, and tarpon fishing here is a catch-and-release-only fishery; every tarpon encountered in this tagging programme is released
